cities.d: The capital, if only in name, hosting the parliament and a unique Afro-Portuguese heritage

x.around: Traffic isn't overwhelming as in Cotonou. However, like Cotonou, the best way and easiest way to see Porto Novo is by zemidjan.

hidden.d: This is an interesting museum that takes an intensive look into the past of Porto Novo’s kings. Displaying a good selection of fetishes, old Yourba king masks, costumes, and some musical instruments, this is definitely worth the…

Former residence of King Toffa. Well maintained, rather simple, palace is a nice look into how Beninese royalty really lived. 1883 was the year King Toffa signed the treaty with French, agreeing to hand over land.

x.intro: Porto-Novo is the capital of Benin, located on the coast in the southeastern part of the country. Benin’s second largest city of approximately 250,000 people is a nice change of pace from the bustling Cotonou and has many nice features.

must.d: The mosque was established in 1925 with chapel architectural style.

cities.d: The pre-colonial capital whose Royal Palaces are on the UNESCO World Heritage List

x.around: Zemi-johns are a popular, cheap and efficient way to get around. They are simply a scooter-like taxi popular in the country.

hidden.d: Houses a number of artefacts and relics from the area. Some of the banners show torture and war tactics of the former Kingdom. The throne of Ghezo is exhibited, which was built on top of human skulls.

cities.d: Benin's largest city and de facto capital, the hectic and cramped home to many government offices and the country's port

x.around: Conventional drop taxis taking you directly to your destination like you might find in New York or London are not the norm in Benin - most taxi drivers wait at fixed intersections for passengers willing to rent the entire vehicle.

hidden.d: You can enter this old Lockheed L-1011 Tristar which the owner has parked on the beach
Another beach with the well-known namesake and even a sign of him if you want a photo op. This beach is a little dirtier than the other, and also subject to strong surf and security considerations.
Interesting stretch in that you have an Airbus A300 parked in the sand behind you. May be a little dirty. Just west of here is an extensive beach called Fidjrosse Beach (Plage De Fidjrosse).
The Institut Français is a fixture of the Cotonou cultural scene, holding concerts, film screenings, theater, stand-up comedy, and more.
The national stadium of Benin and anchor of a sports complex, Stade de l'Amitié hosts not only football matches, but also concerts and markets on the adjacent esplanade and parking lots.
Statue to honor the Agodjié (Amazone) women warriors of Abomey, Kingdom of Dahomey, as popularized in the movie The Woman King.
A big North Korean-built monument to those who died fighting against colonialism. Hosts artists, a food truck, and occasional public concerts.
A bizarre Cold War anachronism, this traffic circle features a larger-than-life statue - seemingly rising out of nowhere - of Bulgaria's first Communist leader, Georgi Dimitrov.

x.intro: Cotonou is the largest city in Benin and the country's primary port of entry for visitors. The city is in the south of the country, on the coastline.

must.d: Noted for its distinct burgundy and white striped tile architecture. The cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Cotonou.

n.es: Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Misericordia de Cotonú
n.it: cattedrale di Nostra Signora della Misericordia

must.d: Run by one of Benin's first families (current head Lionel was defeated in a presidential election in 2016), the Fondation Zinsou is devoted to showing contemporary art in Benin and providing supporting arts education for…

A roundabout that is another tribute to Benin's communist past in the form of a large red star, but you are probably better able to see it from a plane if you get the chance upon departure or arrival.

next.d: the religious centre of Voudoun in the area and a historic city for the slave trade, at 45-60 minutes car ride from Cotonou.
official capital city of Benin with several museums, cultural centres, a royal palace and a historic mosque, at 60 minutes car ride from Cotonou.
UNESCO world heritage site with a number of mud-brick palaces and museums

cities.d: A sleepy beach resort town close to the Togolese border

x.around: Grand Popo has very little traffic. You can pick up a zem (usually wearing a green shirt and baseball cap, but not always) easily at the carrefour, but sometimes, you’ll have to wait a while to get one on the side of the road. Walking is also a good option as most restaurants and hotels are located on a main stretch of road.

cities.d: A border town with Niger, with not much else besides a border post
Largest city on the way to northern Togo or Burkina Faso and a jumping-off point for exploring the Tata Somba
A former slave-trading port that is a center for the country's vodun heritage

hidden.d: A restored slave traders mansion, now a memorial.

x.intro: Ouidah is a city in Southern Benin known for its Voodoo culture and slave-trade history.

must.d: The fort was built by the Portuguese when tapping into the Atlantic slave trade. When slavery was legally abolished, the fort was abandoned until 1865 when it was reoccupied by the Portuguese.

n.en: Fort of São João Baptista de Ajudá
n.it: Forte di São João Baptista de Ajudá

must.d: Located in the fort. Showcases the archaeology, history and arts of Ouidah.

cities.d: The largest city in the central region and the capital of the Borgou Department

intro: For the city in Edo State, see Benin City Benin is a country in West Africa. You'll find culture through a large collection of palatial ruins and temples of the once powerful Kingdom of Dahomey (1800s–1894). Moreover, Benin is the birthplace of Vodun (Voodoo) and all that goes with it. Vodun is the official religion of the country, and an important part of the life of ordinary Beninese. Many important tourist sites are linked to Vodun or the slave trade.

x.intro: W National Park is a trans-border park, with the most important areas in Southwestern Niger, around a meander in the River Niger shaped like the letter W.
x.safe: Caution recommended given rising destabilisation and unrest in eastern Burkina Faso since 2018. As of 2024, Niger is also unsafe due to civil unrest.
